title: Deployment and Release Management: Canary, Blue-Green, Rolling
bodyMarkdown:
## Why release strategy is an operations topic

Most outages follow a change. The operational excellence pillar's [automate and manage change](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/operational-excellence/automate-and-manage-change) guidance therefore combines infrastructure as code, version control, CI/CD, configuration management and automated tests with "controlled rollout mechanisms". Choosing a release strategy is choosing how much of your user base a bad release can hurt, how fast you can detect it, and how fast you can undo it.

## The strategies compared

| Strategy | How it works | Versions live at once | Rollback speed | Extra capacity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Recreate** | Stop all old, then start new | One at a time, with downtime in between | Slow (redeploy) | None | Dev/test, or when two versions cannot coexist and downtime is acceptable |
| **Rolling** | Replace instances gradually | Both during the update | Moderate (roll forward/back gradually) | Small surge | Stateless services, zero downtime with backward-compatible changes |
| **Blue-green** | Build a full parallel (green) environment, validate it, switch traffic atomically | Only one serving at a time | Near-instant (switch back) | Full second environment | Strict no-mixed-versions constraints, instant rollback |
| **Canary** | Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, measure, expand | Both, deliberately | Fast (shift percentage to zero) | Small | High-traffic services where you want real-user evidence with limited blast radius |
| **A/B test** | Split by user cohort to compare behavior | Both, by design | n/a | Varies | Product experiments, not a release safety mechanism |

The decision criteria the exam uses:

- **Cannot tolerate two versions serving at once and needs instant rollback:** blue-green with a validated standby and an atomic switch.
- **Wants real traffic evidence, limited blast radius, automatic promotion or rollback:** canary with automated verification.
- **Stateless fleet, zero downtime, no extra environment:** rolling update.
- **Downtime acceptable, simplest possible:** recreate.

Blue-green's cost is a second full environment and, if a database schema is shared, a migration that both versions can live with (expand and contract). Canary's cost is the complexity of routing, observability and decision logic.

## Continuous integration and quality gates

[Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/overview) runs a build as a series of steps, each in its own container, from a YAML or JSON config that holds dependencies, tests, analyses and artifact creation. Default pools are public Google-managed workers; **private pools** are dedicated and can reach private network resources. [Triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers) fire on a branch push, a new tag, a pull request or manually. Included-files and ignored-files globs limit which changes build (ignored wins), a trigger can require **approval** before it runs, and only the trigger's own service account is used (one named in the build config is ignored), so give it least privilege.

Quality control means automated gates, not a person eyeballing a release. The framework lists unit, integration and end-to-end tests as part of change automation. Order them cheap to expensive: static checks and unit tests on every pull request, with human code review required before merge; integration tests against the built artifact; a vulnerability scan; then end-to-end tests and Cloud Deploy verification in staging. A failed gate stops the release. A test that only runs after the production deploy is monitoring, not quality control, and skipping the pipeline for a "quick hotfix" removes the gates exactly when risk is highest.

## Supply-chain gates

[Artifact Registry](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/overview) stores images and packages in standard repositories, caches upstream sources in remote repositories, and groups repositories behind one virtual endpoint with search priorities. [Artifact Analysis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/artifact-analysis) scans images automatically on every push to Artifact Registry and keeps vulnerability data current; on-demand scans of local images are point-in-time and not refreshed. [Binary Authorization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) enforces at deploy time on GKE and Cloud Run (also Cloud Service Mesh and Google Distributed Cloud): the policy requires **attestations** from trusted **attestors**, for example one that Cloud Build issues after tests and provenance pass. Dry-run mode logs violations without blocking, break-glass covers emergencies, and continuous validation checks running Pods. Scanning detects and Binary Authorization prevents, so a scan nobody gates on does not protect production, and pulling images straight from public registries bypasses both.

## GitOps and feature flags

### Pull versus push delivery

| | Push (Cloud Build `kubectl apply`, Cloud Deploy) | Pull (Config Sync) |
|---|---|---|
| Who applies | A pipeline outside the cluster, holding credentials to it | A reconciler inside the cluster that pulls the source |
| When it acts | Only when triggered: a merge, a release, a promotion | Continuously |
| Hand edits (drift) | Stay until the next run overwrites them | Detected and reverted |
| CI system down | Nothing reaches the cluster | The cluster still converges to the last committed state |
| Strength | Ordered targets, approvals, canary, verification | Convergence and consistency across many clusters |

[Config Sync](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/overview) is GitOps for GKE: a Git repository (or an OCI image or Helm chart in Artifact Registry) is the single source of truth, and clusters are continuously reconciled to it, which corrects drift. The [architecture](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/concepts/architecture) is a reconciler in the cluster for each RootSync or RepoSync object, with git-sync, helm-sync or oci-sync containers fetching the source. Cluster-scoped sync carries shared config and policies, namespace-scoped sync carries tenant RBAC. The [drift guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/how-to/prevent-config-drift) says Config Sync "automatically detects and reverts drift" and that you cannot disable this self-healing. Two limits: it covers only fields your source specifies (unspecified fields may drift), and the optional drift-prevention admission webhook, which blocks conflicting changes up front, can cause high memory use in clusters with many CRDs.

[Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) is the push side: your CI calls it to create a release, promotion deploys to the next target, and an approval can be required for promotion to any target. It does not watch Git or the cluster. Choose Config Sync for continuous, multi-cluster convergence of cluster configuration, with rollback by reverting a commit; choose Cloud Deploy for ordered promotion with approvals, canary and verification of application releases.

### Rolling back in each model

- **Config Sync:** revert the commit in the synced repository and the reconciler applies the previous state. A hand edit to a specified field, including `kubectl edit` or `kubectl rollout undo`, is reconciled away within moments, so it is not a rollback.
- **Break-glass:** the [stop and resume guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/how-to/stopping-resuming-syncing) sets `spec.configSync.stopSyncing` to `true` (manual installs scale the reconcilers to zero), and you resume afterward. To exempt one object, commit the annotation `configmanagement.gke.io/managed: disabled` ([managing objects](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/how-to/managing-objects)).
- **Cloud Deploy:** a new rollout of the last successful release.
- **Cloud Run:** `gcloud run services update-traffic SERVICE --to-revisions REVISION=100` points traffic at an existing revision. The routing configuration updates immediately, it needs no redeploy, and it does not re-run deployment health checks (the traffic shift itself is not instantaneous, as noted under Cloud Run below).

### Who sees the change: canary, feature flag or API version

| Mechanism | Exposure is decided by | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Canary | A traffic percentage (Cloud Run and Cloud Deploy split by percentage, not by named client) | The risk is the build itself |
| Feature flag | The application, per request, using targeting rules on user or request attributes | One feature's behavior, or a named cohort such as pilot tenants |
| API version | The client, by calling a versioned path | A breaking contract change that clients adopt on their own schedule |

[App Lifecycle Manager feature flags](https://docs.cloud.google.com/saas-runtime/docs/flags/flags-overview) (Preview when reviewed) decouple release from deployment: ship code with the feature off, enable it gradually, and roll back by disabling the flag instead of redeploying. Targeting uses Common Expression Language rules on user or request attributes, applications read flags through an OpenFeature SDK with the flagd provider, and flag changes go live only through a rollout. Use a flag when the risk is one feature's behavior and a canary when the risk is the build itself. Know the criterion, not the product name: a named cohort needs a flag, a percentage needs a canary.

## Cloud Deploy

[Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) is a managed continuous delivery service that automates delivery to a series of target environments in a defined promotion sequence. Key objects:

- **Delivery pipeline:** the ordered sequence of targets (for example dev, staging, prod).
- **Target:** a GKE cluster, a Cloud Run service, or a GKE attached cluster.
- **Release:** the rendered manifests for a version. Creating one automatically creates a rollout to the first target.
- **Rollout:** the deployment of a release to one target. Promotion creates the next rollout.

It uses **Skaffold** to render, deploy and verify. Cloud Deploy accepts artifacts from any CI system and repository; Cloud Build is the usual CI partner. Promotions can be gated with `requireApproval`, and it publishes Pub/Sub notifications for approvals and deployment events. A rollback is a new rollout of the last successful release to the target.

### Strategies

The [deployment strategies page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies) lists two built-in strategies: **standard** (direct deployment, no progressive rollout) and **canary**. Canary is supported across the runtimes Cloud Deploy targets. Progression percentages are whole numbers you choose, and for Cloud Run a 50% canary sends half the traffic to the new revision and half to the old. A canary needs an existing deployed version to reference; the first deployment to a target can skip canary phases. Both strategies support rollback, rollout cancellation and parallel deployment to several targets. The Well-Architected framework also lists blue-green deployments, traffic splitting and rollbacks among Cloud Deploy's capabilities, so expect blue-green to appear alongside it.

### Verification

[Deployment verification](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/verify-deployment) is configured with a `verify` stanza on a target. You supply test containers; exit code 0 means success, non-zero means failure, and if several containers run they must all succeed. A failed verification fails the rollout. You can retry a failed verify job with `gcloud deploy rollouts retry-job`. On GKE, verification can run on the application cluster through Skaffold; for Cloud Run it runs in the Cloud Deploy execution environment, not on the service. A verification container can query metrics (for example Cloud Monitoring error rate or latency against the stable version) and exit non-zero when thresholds are breached; that is a design you build, not a built-in SLO comparison.

### Automation and auto-rollback

[Cloud Deploy automation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/automation) provides four rule types: promote release automatically after a successful rollout (with optional delay), scheduled promotion on a cron schedule, **advance rollout** (canary only: move automatically to the next phase after success) and **repair rollout** (retry a failed rollout). If retries are exhausted, repair can create a new rollout that **rolls back to the most recent successful release**. Automations are YAML applied with `gcloud deploy apply`, tied to one delivery pipeline, with a maximum of 250 automation rules per pipeline. The combination "canary + verification + advance rollout + repair rollout with rollback" is the managed answer to "expose a small slice, check health, roll back with no human".

## Native mechanisms per runtime

### Compute Engine managed instance groups

A [MIG rolling update](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/updating-migs) replaces VMs with a new instance template. Update type is **proactive** (the MIG applies changes automatically at the speed and disruption level you set) or **opportunistic** (changes apply only to the VMs you manually target). **maxSurge** is how many extra VMs may be created during the update, and **maxUnavailable** is how many may be down; together they set your disruption budget. The replacement method is **substitute** (create replacements before removing old VMs) or **recreate**. A **min-ready** time controls how long a new VM must be healthy before the update continues. A **canary update** applies a second instance template to a subset of VMs before full rollout.

### GKE and Kubernetes Deployments

A Kubernetes [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) defaults to the **RollingUpdate** strategy with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` of 25% each; **Recreate** terminates all pods first (downtime, but no version mixing). `kubectl rollout undo` reverts to a prior revision, and the default `revisionHistoryLimit` of 10 keeps old ReplicaSets available. Readiness probes gate traffic to new pods, which is what makes a rolling update safe.

### Cloud Run

[Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration) creates a new revision per deployment. You can split traffic by percentage across revisions (percentages must total 100%), do gradual rollouts, give revisions tags for test URLs at 0% traffic, and roll back by directing traffic to a previous revision. In-flight requests are not dropped during traffic changes. Traffic changes are not instantaneous. This makes canary and rollback on Cloud Run a configuration change, no extra tooling.

## Scenario walk-through

Apply the criteria in order. First, can two versions serve traffic at once? If not, choose blue-green (or recreate if downtime is acceptable). If so, do you need production evidence before full exposure? If yes, canary with an automated comparison against the stable version and promotion or rollback without a human; if not, a rolling update with sensible surge and unavailability settings suits a backward-compatible stateless fleet. Finally, who decides to roll back? In an operationally excellent design it is a pre-agreed metric threshold, not whoever notices a dashboard.

A typical end-to-end flow: a commit triggers Cloud Build, which runs tests, pushes an image to Artifact Registry (where Artifact Analysis scans it) and creates a Cloud Deploy release. The release rolls out to dev, then staging, then production through a canary, with Binary Authorization enforcing attestations at deploy time. Verification containers check health at each phase, advance rollout proceeds on success, and repair rollout retries and then rolls back on failure.

## Rollback design

Whatever the strategy, a release is not operationally excellent without a tested rollback:

- Keep the previous artifact, revision or template available.
- Make database changes backward compatible (add first, remove later) so rollback is possible.
- Decide in advance the automated criteria for rollback: error rate, latency percentile, saturation, in line with your SLOs.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Manually editing production YAML and watching logs.** No repeatability, no verification, no audit trail.
- **Canary with no automated comparison.** A canary that no one measures is just a slow rollout.
- **Cutting 100% over at once and calling it canary.** Blue-green is a switch, not a gradual shift.
- **Recreate for a customer-facing service.** It guarantees downtime.
- **Ignoring data compatibility.** A schema change that breaks the old version makes rollback a data-loss decision.
- **Treating one-time approvals as safety.** Approval gates help, but automated verification scales.
- **Scanning images but never gating deployment**, or letting a trigger's service account hold broad project roles.
- **Long-lived feature flags** that are never removed, or flags used to hide a schema change the old version cannot read.
- **Hand-fixing a GitOps cluster.** The reconciler reverts the fix; commit the change, or use the documented stop-sync break-glass and resume.
- **Push-only pipelines for cluster configuration.** Drift persists between runs, and a CI outage freezes the fleet.
- **A percentage canary for a named customer.** Splits are by share of traffic, so the customer may or may not see the change.

## Exam tips

- **Canary with automated verification.** Small percentage of traffic, compare error rate to stable, promote only if healthy: Cloud Deploy canary plus verification.
- **Blue-green for no mixed versions plus instant rollback.** Validate the standby fully, then switch atomically; the cost is double capacity.
- **MIG rolling update uses maxSurge and maxUnavailable.** Zero-downtime for stateless MIGs behind a load balancer; never delete and recreate the group or SSH into VMs.
- **Full automation answer.** Cloud Deploy canary, verify job gated on health checks, advance rollout and repair rollout with rollback to the last successful release.
- **Cloud Run rollbacks are traffic moves.** Split by percentage across revisions, tag for test URLs, redirect to a prior revision to roll back: no rebuild, no redeploy.
- **Recreate means downtime.** Choose it only when downtime is acceptable.
- **Cloud Deploy targets.** GKE, Cloud Run and GKE attached clusters, with Skaffold underneath.
- **Rollback must be automated and tested.** Pick answers that define criteria in advance over answers that depend on humans noticing.
- **Quality control is automated gates.** Unit tests and required code review on pull requests, integration tests and a vulnerability scan on the artifact, then staging verification; a failed gate stops the release.
- **Scan detects, Binary Authorization prevents.** Artifact Analysis scans on every push to Artifact Registry; Binary Authorization blocks deployment of images without attestations from trusted attestors (dry-run first).
- **Pull versus push.** Config Sync reconciles clusters to Git: as an in-cluster reconciler it reverts drift and keeps working when CI is down. Push pipelines (Cloud Build `kubectl apply`, Cloud Deploy) act only when triggered. Cloud Deploy stays right for staged promotion with approvals.
- **GitOps rollback is a revert.** Revert the commit in the synced repository; hand edits (`kubectl edit`, `rollout undo`) are reconciled away. Stopping sync or marking an object unmanaged is break-glass.
- **Cohort versus percentage.** A canary splits by percentage and cannot name a client; a feature flag with targeting rules exposes a named cohort and rolls back by switching off, without redeploying. A breaking contract change calls for a new API version instead.
